primary_claim: Training cross-layer transcoders to be sparsely-connected (via a learned binary mask on virtual weights) yields reconstruction error that decreases with the number of connections per latent, and the resulting latents and connections are often, though not always, interpretable.

effect.metric: excess FVU (fraction of variance unexplained) vs. number of connections C
effect.value: FVU decreases as C increases but excess FVU plateaus at a still-high level due to compounding reconstruction errors

contradicts_or_qualifies: Notes Lucius Bushnaq's argument that the feature-splitting issue observed here may be a deep, possibly unavoidable problem with SAEs generally

Contrasts with Farnik et al (2025) Jacobian SAEs, whose notion of sparse connectivity is a weaker, linear-approximation, context-dependent form rather than the exact, context-independent sparsity trained for here
stated_future_work: Use AuxK loss or resample dead latents, and experiment with initialization/learning rate to fix dead-latent issue
Include contributions from upstream SAE errors (detaching them from the computational graph) to reduce excess FVU
Restrict masking to co-occurrence-derived candidate connections after an initial dense-training phase, to reduce memory from O(F^2 L^2) to O(FL^2)
Detach upstream feature activations before applying virtual weights to reduce memory from O(L^2F^2) to O(F^2)
Use Matryoshka BatchTopK SAEs to mitigate feature splitting
limitations_stated: Many latents die during training, hurting reconstruction and monosemanticity
Excess FVU remains high even without masking, due to compounding reconstruction errors across layers
Memory scales as O(F^2 L^2), prohibiting scaling to large models
Feature splitting persists: dictionaries find many granular features instead of a single computationally-relevant one
Attention patterns are borrowed from the original model rather than sparsified, a deficiency of the approach
quote: Reconstruction error decreases with $C$, as expected. Furthermore, latents and connections are often (but not always) interpretable: a few non-cherry-picked case studies are shown below.
